explanation: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, AML M3 subtype) is characterized by t(15;17), forming PML-RARA fusion gene which blocks myeloid differentiation. Auer rods are abundant, and DIC is a major risk. ATRA (retinoic acid) induces differentiation of leukemic promyelocytes.

question: A 9-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish boy is evaluated for progressive leg pain, bone crises, and easy bruising. Physical examination reveals massive splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly. CBC demonstrates Hb 8.4 g/dL, WBC 3,200/mm³, and platelets 68,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspirate reveals large, engorged macrophages with fibrillary cytoplasm resembling crumpled tissue paper. A defect in which of the following lysosomal enzymes is the primary cause of this patient's presentation? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P162)
explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease, caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase (beta-glucosidase). This leads to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages ('Gaucher cells'), causing hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and bone lesions (aseptic necrosis, Erlenmeyer flask deformity).

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 169: Deficiency of which glycogen breakdown enzyme causes severe exercise-induced muscle cramps, rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobinuria without hypoglycemia?
explanation: McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V) is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Patients present with exercise intolerance, muscle cramping, and myoglobinuria due to rhabdomyolysis. The venous lactate flatline on forearm ischemic test is characteristic.

question: A 4-year-old unimmunized girl brought from an immigrant settlement presents with severe sore throat, fever, and cervical lymphadenopathy ('bull neck'). Oropharyngeal exam reveals a thick, grayish pseudomembrane adhering tightly to the soft palate that bleeds upon gentle scraping. ECG shows first-degree AV block. Which exotoxin mechanism accounts for the cardiac and nerve tissue toxicity seen in this infection? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P176)
option_a: Inactivation of 60S ribosomal subunit via N-glycosidase activity
option_b: Direct lecithinase activity disrupting host cell membranes
option_c: Cleavage of SNARE proteins inhibiting GABA release
option_d: Overactivation of adenylate cyclase via Gs alpha subunit ADP-ribosylation
explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces diphtheria toxin, an A-B exotoxin that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF-2), halting protein synthesis and causing cell death. Tissue destruction leads to pseudomembrane formation, myocarditis, and cranial nerve palsies.

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 183: Rupture of the interventricular septum leading to a acute left-to-right shunt and pansystolic murmur typically occurs how many days after an acute myocardial infarction?
option_a: Acute mitral valve regurgitation due to papillary muscle rupture
option_b: Left ventricular free wall rupture with tamponade
explanation: Interventricular septal rupture occurs 3-5 days post-MI due to macrophage-mediated tissue degradation. It presents with sudden cardiogenic shock, a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, and an O2 saturation step-up from right atrium to right ventricle.

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with facial swelling, dark cola-colored urine, and leg edema 2 weeks after recovering from impetigo. Exam shows BP 142/90 mmHg. Urinalysis demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells, RBC casts, and 2+ proteinuria. Serum C3 complement level is significantly decreased. Electron microscopy of renal biopsy demonstrates large subepithelial immune complex humps. What is the most likely diagnosis? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P190)
explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows group A streptococcal skin or pharyngeal infection. It features nephritic syndrome (hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, edema, low C3) with characteristic subepithelial 'hump-like' deposits on EM.

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 197: Which class III antiarrhythmic blocks cardiac potassium channels, exhibits class I, II, and IV properties, and requires baseline pulmonary function and thyroid tests?
explanation: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic (K+ channel blocker) with properties of all 4 antiarrhythmic classes. Its notable adverse effects include pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism due to high iodine content), corneal microdeposits, hepatotoxicity, and blue-gray skin discoloration.

question: A 61-year-old male smoker suddenly develops dizziness, hoarseness, dysphagia, and loss of balance. Physical examination reveals ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face, ataxia of the right upper extremity, and loss of pain and temperature on the left trunk and limbs. Gag reflex is absent on the right. An ischemic stroke in which vascular territory is the cause? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P204)
explanation: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) occlusion causes Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome. Nucleus ambiguus damage causes dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of gag reflex. Vestibular nuclei damage causes vertigo/nystagmus. Spinothalamic tract and trigeminal nucleus damage cause contralateral body and ipsilateral face pain/temp loss.

explanation: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, AML M3 subtype) is characterized by t(15;17), forming PML-RARA fusion gene which blocks myeloid differentiation. Auer rods are abundant, and DIC is a major risk. ATRA (retinoic acid) induces differentiation of leukemic promyelocytes.

question: A 9-year-old Ashkenazi Jewish boy is evaluated for progressive leg pain, bone crises, and easy bruising. Physical examination reveals massive splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly. CBC demonstrates Hb 8.4 g/dL, WBC 3,200/mm³, and platelets 68,000/mm³. Bone marrow aspirate reveals large, engorged macrophages with fibrillary cytoplasm resembling crumpled tissue paper. A defect in which of the following lysosomal enzymes is the primary cause of this patient's presentation? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P88)
explanation: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease, caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of glucocerebrosidase (beta-glucosidase). This leads to accumulation of glucocerebroside in macrophages ('Gaucher cells'), causing hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, and bone lesions (aseptic necrosis, Erlenmeyer flask deformity).

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 95: Deficiency of which glycogen breakdown enzyme causes severe exercise-induced muscle cramps, rhabdomyolysis, and myoglobinuria without hypoglycemia?
explanation: McArdle disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V) is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Patients present with exercise intolerance, muscle cramping, and myoglobinuria due to rhabdomyolysis. The venous lactate flatline on forearm ischemic test is characteristic.

question: A 4-year-old unimmunized girl brought from an immigrant settlement presents with severe sore throat, fever, and cervical lymphadenopathy ('bull neck'). Oropharyngeal exam reveals a thick, grayish pseudomembrane adhering tightly to the soft palate that bleeds upon gentle scraping. ECG shows first-degree AV block. Which exotoxin mechanism accounts for the cardiac and nerve tissue toxicity seen in this infection? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P102)
option_a: Direct lecithinase activity disrupting host cell membranes
option_b: Inactivation of 60S ribosomal subunit via N-glycosidase activity
option_c: Overactivation of adenylate cyclase via Gs alpha subunit ADP-ribosylation
option_e: Cleavage of SNARE proteins inhibiting GABA release
explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces diphtheria toxin, an A-B exotoxin that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 (EF-2), halting protein synthesis and causing cell death. Tissue destruction leads to pseudomembrane formation, myocarditis, and cranial nerve palsies.

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 109: Rupture of the interventricular septum leading to a acute left-to-right shunt and pansystolic murmur typically occurs how many days after an acute myocardial infarction?
option_d: Acute mitral valve regurgitation due to papillary muscle rupture
option_e: Left ventricular free wall rupture with tamponade
explanation: Interventricular septal rupture occurs 3-5 days post-MI due to macrophage-mediated tissue degradation. It presents with sudden cardiogenic shock, a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal border, and an O2 saturation step-up from right atrium to right ventricle.

question: A 7-year-old boy presents with facial swelling, dark cola-colored urine, and leg edema 2 weeks after recovering from impetigo. Exam shows BP 142/90 mmHg. Urinalysis demonstrates dysmorphic red blood cells, RBC casts, and 2+ proteinuria. Serum C3 complement level is significantly decreased. Electron microscopy of renal biopsy demonstrates large subepithelial immune complex humps. What is the most likely diagnosis? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P116)
explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows group A streptococcal skin or pharyngeal infection. It features nephritic syndrome (hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, edema, low C3) with characteristic subepithelial 'hump-like' deposits on EM.

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 123: Which class III antiarrhythmic blocks cardiac potassium channels, exhibits class I, II, and IV properties, and requires baseline pulmonary function and thyroid tests?
explanation: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic (K+ channel blocker) with properties of all 4 antiarrhythmic classes. Its notable adverse effects include pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism due to high iodine content), corneal microdeposits, hepatotoxicity, and blue-gray skin discoloration.

question: A 61-year-old male smoker suddenly develops dizziness, hoarseness, dysphagia, and loss of balance. Physical examination reveals ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face, ataxia of the right upper extremity, and loss of pain and temperature on the left trunk and limbs. Gag reflex is absent on the right. An ischemic stroke in which vascular territory is the cause? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P130)
explanation: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) occlusion causes Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome. Nucleus ambiguus damage causes dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of gag reflex. Vestibular nuclei damage causes vertigo/nystagmus. Spinothalamic tract and trigeminal nucleus damage cause contralateral body and ipsilateral face pain/temp loss.

Electron microscopy of renal biopsy demonstrates large subepithelial immune complex humps. What is the most likely diagnosis? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P732)
explanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) follows group A streptococcal skin or pharyngeal infection. It features nephritic syndrome (hematuria, RBC casts, hypertension, edema, low C3) with characteristic subepithelial 'hump-like' deposits on EM.

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 739: Which class III antiarrhythmic blocks cardiac potassium channels, exhibits class I, II, and IV properties, and requires baseline pulmonary function and thyroid tests?
explanation: Amiodarone is a Class III antiarrhythmic (K+ channel blocker) with properties of all 4 antiarrhythmic classes. Its notable adverse effects include pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism due to high iodine content), corneal microdeposits, hepatotoxicity, and blue-gray skin discoloration.

question: A 61-year-old male smoker suddenly develops dizziness, hoarseness, dysphagia, and loss of balance. Physical examination reveals ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), loss of pain and temperature sensation on the right side of the face, ataxia of the right upper extremity, and loss of pain and temperature on the left trunk and limbs. Gag reflex is absent on the right. An ischemic stroke in which vascular territory is the cause? (Clinical case protocol FA-2023-P746)
explanation: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) occlusion causes Lateral Medullary (Wallenberg) Syndrome. Nucleus ambiguus damage causes dysphagia, hoarseness, and loss of gag reflex. Vestibular nuclei damage causes vertigo/nystagmus. Spinothalamic tract and trigeminal nucleus damage cause contralateral body and ipsilateral face pain/temp loss.

question: Regarding USMLE Step 1 High-Yield concept on Page 753: Which translocation t(15;17) creates the PML-RARA fusion protein and responds to All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA)?
option_d: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) plus arsenic trioxide
explanation: Acute Promyelocytic Leukemia (APL, AML M3 subtype) is characterized by t(15;17), forming PML-RARA fusion gene which blocks myeloid differentiation. Auer rods are abundant, and DIC is a major risk. ATRA (retinoic acid) induces differentiation of leukemic promyelocytes.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1000)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 21): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1002)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 43): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrent perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows deep longitudinal ulcers separated by normal mucosa ('skip lesions') and a 'cobblestone' mucosa in the terminal ileum. Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1004)
option_a: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
option_c: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
option_d: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
option_e: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 65): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1006)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 87): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1008)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 109): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1140)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 722): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1142)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 744): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrent perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows deep longitudinal ulcers separated by normal mucosa ('skip lesions') and a 'cobblestone' mucosa in the terminal ileum. Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1144)
option_a: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
option_b: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
option_c: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
option_e: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 766): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1146)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 788): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1148)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 810): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1188)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 411): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1190)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 433): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1192)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 455): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrent perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows deep longitudinal ulcers separated by normal mucosa ('skip lesions') and a 'cobblestone' mucosa in the terminal ileum. Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1194)
option_b: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
option_c: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
option_d: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
option_e: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 477): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1196)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 499): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1284)
option_a: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
option_b: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
option_d: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
option_e: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 628): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1286)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 650): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1288)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 672): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1290)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 694): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1292)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 716): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1666)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 635): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1668)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 657): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1670)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 679): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1672)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 701): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrent perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows deep longitudinal ulcers separated by normal mucosa ('skip lesions') and a 'cobblestone' mucosa in the terminal ileum. Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1674)
option_a: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
option_b: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
option_d: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
option_e: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 723): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1762)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 13): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrent perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows deep longitudinal ulcers separated by normal mucosa ('skip lesions') and a 'cobblestone' mucosa in the terminal ileum. Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1764)
option_a: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
option_b: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
option_d: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
option_e: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 35): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1766)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 57): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1768)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 79): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1770)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 101): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1954)
option_a: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
option_b: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
option_d: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
option_e: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 447): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1956)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 469): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1958)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 491): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. Echocardiogram confirms a structural cardiovascular lesion. What embryological structure failed to close or regress in this patient? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1960)
explanation: Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) causes a continuous machine-like murmur. When severe pulmonary hypertension develops (Eisenmenger syndrome), unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left through the PDA into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, resulting in differential cyanosis (cyanotic lower extremities with normal pink upper body).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 513): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #1962)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 535): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 360): Which class IB antiarrhythmic agent selectively binds to depolarized or ischemic sodium channels and has the lowest risk of QTc prolongation?
explanation: Lidocaine (Class IB antiarrhythmic) selectively acts on depolarized/ischemic sodium channels and rapidly dissociates from channels in normal state (state-dependent binding). It shortens action potential duration and is highly effective for ischemic ventricular arrhythmias without prolonging QTc.

question: A 12-day-old female neonate presents to the emergency department with lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting. Physical exam shows hyperpigmented skin and ambiguous genitalia with clitoromegaly. Blood pressure is 55/35 mmHg. Serum labs reveal Na+ 118 mEq/L, K+ 7.2 mEq/L, glucose 45 mg/dL. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated. Deficiency of which of the following adrenal enzymes is responsible? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #2482)
explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) cases. Inability to synthesize aldosterone and cortisol leads to salt-wasting crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia) and elevated ACTH which shunts progesterone precursors into androgen synthesis, virilizing female infants.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 382): Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain) is characterized by painful thyroid enlargement, transient hyperthyroidism, and which biopsy finding?
explanation: Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis follows a viral illness and presents with a tender thyroid, elevated ESR, hyperthyroidism due to stored hormone release, and characteristically low radioactive iodine uptake (<1%). Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells.

question: A 26-year-old man presents with chronic non-bloody diarrhea, right lower quadrant abdominal pain, weight loss, and recurrent perianal fistulae. Colonoscopy shows deep longitudinal ulcers separated by normal mucosa ('skip lesions') and a 'cobblestone' mucosa in the terminal ileum. Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates transmural inflammation and noncaseating granulomas. Which complication is this patient at highest risk of developing? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #2484)
option_a: Pseudomembranous colitis secondary to C. difficile toxin
option_b: Strictures and bowel obstruction due to transmural fibrosis
option_c: Primary sclerosing cholangitis with p-ANCA positivity
option_e: Widespread diffuse mucosal adenocarcinoma of the rectosigmoid
explanation: Crohn disease is characterized by transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, skip lesions, creeping fat, and cobblestoning. Because inflammation involves all intestinal layers, healing results in transmural fibrosis, leading to strictures, bowel obstruction, and fistula formation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 404): Wilson disease results from mutations in ATP7B leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia (lenticular nucleus), and cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings). What is the expected serum ceruloplasmin level?
explanation: Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive defect in copper-transporting ATPase (ATP7B gene). Impaired copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and reduced biliary excretion result in decreased serum ceruloplasmin levels, elevated free serum copper, and copper accumulation in liver, brain, and cornea.

question: A 58-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and diabetic nephropathy presents for routine follow-up. Serum chemistry demonstrates Na+ 137 mEq/L, K+ 5.8 mEq/L, Cl- 108 mEq/L, HCO3- 17 mEq/L, and BUN 32 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas confirms a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Urinalysis shows a urine pH of 4.8. Plasma renin and aldosterone levels are both low. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is present? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #2486)
explanation: Type 4 RTA is hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, most commonly seen in diabetic nephropathy. Deficiency or resistance to aldosterone impairs K+ and H+ secretion in the collecting duct, causing hyperkalemia and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Unlike Types 1 and 2, urine pH remains acidic (<5.5).

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 426): Which neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein and extracellular amyloid-beta plaques?
explanation: Alzheimer disease pathology features extracellular senile/amyloid plaques (A-beta 42 peptides) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein (a microtubule-stabilizing protein).

question: A 4-month-old male infant presents with persistent oral candidiasis, severe chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. CBC reveals severe lymphopenia (absolute lymphocyte count 400/mm³). Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of T cells and NK cells, with dysfunctional B cells. A mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain subunit is identified. What is the mode of inheritance of this immunodeficiency? (Ref: FA-Step1 Case Protocol #2488)
explanation: The most common form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is X-linked recessive SCID, caused by mutations in IL2RG (common gamma chain of IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 receptors). This prevents T cell and NK cell maturation.

question: High-Yield Mechanism (First Aid 2023 Page 448): Which antidote is administered for organophosphate insecticide poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase at neuromuscular junctions?
explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, bradycardia, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) but does NOT reverse nicotinic neuromuscular blockade. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) regenerates active acetylcholinesterase at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors if given before enzyme 'aging'.

question: A 16-year-old female presents for a sports physical. She is asymptomatic but examination reveals BP of 124/60 mmHg in the right upper extremity. Auscultation demonstrates a continuous machine-like murmur best heard at the left infraclavicular area. Pulse oximetry reveals 98% saturation in the right hand but 87% in both feet. question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #1]: Which enzyme deficiency in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt results in episodic intravascular hemolysis, Heinz bodies, and bite cells following oxidative stress (e.g., fava beans, primaquine, infection)?
explanation: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder impairing NADPH generation in the HMP shunt. Without NADPH, glutathione cannot be reduced, leaving erythrocytes vulnerable to oxidative stress. Hemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies, which are phagocytosed by splenic macrophages creating bite cells.

question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the pediatric clinic with recurrent hemarthrosis of the right knee following minor trauma. Family history is notable for maternal uncles with bleeding tendencies. Laboratory evaluation reveals PT 12 seconds (normal), aPTT 68 seconds (significantly prolonged), and platelet count 250,000/mm³. Mixing study with normal plasma completely corrects the aPTT. A deficiency in which factor is the cause of this patient's bleeding disorder? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-2]
explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII in the intrinsic coagulation pathway, resulting in a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with normal prothrombin time (PT) and normal bleeding time. Mixing studies correct aPTT by supplying Factor VIII.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #3]: Which mechanism of genetic exchange in influenza viruses (segmented RNA genome) leads to major antigenic shifts responsible for global pandemics?
option_d: Point mutation leading to antigenic drift
option_e: Recombination via template switching during reverse transcription
explanation: Antigenic shift occurs when two different influenza strains co-infect the same host cell, leading to reassortment of their segmented RNA genomes. This creates novel hemagglutinin or neuraminidase surface antigens to which the human population has no immunity, causing pandemics.

question: A 68-year-old active woman being treated for a complicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa urinary tract infection presents to the clinic complaining of sudden onset left ankle pain and swelling. Examination reveals exquisite tenderness over the Achilles tendon, and Thompson test is weakly positive. Which antibiotic class prescribed for her infection is directly associated with tendonitis and tendon rupture? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-4]
explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV. They carry a black box warning for tendonitis and tendon rupture (most commonly the Achilles tendon), especially in elderly patients, organ transplant recipients, and those taking corticosteroids.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #5]: Which autoimmune connective tissue disorder presents with heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and symmetrical proximal muscle weakness with anti-Jo-1 antibodies?
explanation: Dermatomyositis is a CD4+ T cell-mediated perimysial autoimmune inflammatory myopathy. Clinical hallmarks include proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and shawl sign. Lab findings include elevated CK and positive anti-Jo-1 or anti-Mi-2 antibodies.

question: A 32-year-old non-smoking male accountant presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and wheezing. Family history reveals a maternal uncle who died of liver cirrhosis in his 40s. Chest CT demonstrates panacinar emphysema predominantly involving the lower lobes of both lungs. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules within hepatocytes. A deficiency of which circulating protein causes this combined pulmonary and hepatic pathology? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-6]
explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ genotype) results in uninhibited neutrophil elastase activity, destroying lung parenchyma (panacinar emphysema, lower lobe predominant). Misfolded AAT protein accumulates in liver endoplasmic reticulum, presenting as PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules and liver cirrhosis.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #7]: Which personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, alongside marked impulsivity and splitting defense mechanisms?
option_c: Splitting (categorizing people as all good or all bad)
explanation: Borderline Personality Disorder is characterized by instability in mood, self-image, and relationships, impulsivity, recurrent suicidal gestures, and chronic emptiness. Splitting (viewing individuals as strictly all-good or all-bad) is the primary defense mechanism.

question: An 18-year-old woman is evaluated for lower abdominal distension and pelvic pain. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a 9 cm solid ovarian mass. Serum beta-hCG is mildly elevated, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is markedly increased, while AFP is normal. Histopathology of the resected tumor demonstrates sheets of large uniform cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm and central round nuclei separated by fibrous septa infiltrated with lymphocytes ('fried egg' appearance). What is the diagnosis? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-8]
explanation: Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant germ cell tumor in young females (equivalent to male seminoma). Histology shows clear 'fried egg' cells with lymphocytic stroma. Tumor markers include elevated LDH and hCG.

explanation: Borderline Personality Disorder is characterized by instability in mood, self-image, and relationships, impulsivity, recurrent suicidal gestures, and chronic emptiness. Splitting (viewing individuals as strictly all-good or all-bad) is the primary defense mechanism.

question: An 18-year-old woman is evaluated for lower abdominal distension and pelvic pain. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a 9 cm solid ovarian mass. Serum beta-hCG is mildly elevated, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is markedly increased, while AFP is normal. Histopathology of the resected tumor demonstrates sheets of large uniform cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm and central round nuclei separated by fibrous septa infiltrated with lymphocytes ('fried egg' appearance). What is the diagnosis? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-616]
explanation: Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant germ cell tumor in young females (equivalent to male seminoma). Histology shows clear 'fried egg' cells with lymphocytic stroma. Tumor markers include elevated LDH and hCG.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #617]: Which enzyme deficiency in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt results in episodic intravascular hemolysis, Heinz bodies, and bite cells following oxidative stress (e.g., fava beans, primaquine, infection)?
explanation: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder impairing NADPH generation in the HMP shunt. Without NADPH, glutathione cannot be reduced, leaving erythrocytes vulnerable to oxidative stress. Hemoglobin denatures into Heinz bodies, which are phagocytosed by splenic macrophages creating bite cells.

question: An 8-year-old boy presents to the pediatric clinic with recurrent hemarthrosis of the right knee following minor trauma. Family history is notable for maternal uncles with bleeding tendencies. Laboratory evaluation reveals PT 12 seconds (normal), aPTT 68 seconds (significantly prolonged), and platelet count 250,000/mm³. Mixing study with normal plasma completely corrects the aPTT. A deficiency in which factor is the cause of this patient's bleeding disorder? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-618]
explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII in the intrinsic coagulation pathway, resulting in a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with normal prothrombin time (PT) and normal bleeding time. Mixing studies correct aPTT by supplying Factor VIII.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #619]: Which mechanism of genetic exchange in influenza viruses (segmented RNA genome) leads to major antigenic shifts responsible for global pandemics?
option_b: Recombination via template switching during reverse transcription
option_c: Point mutation leading to antigenic drift
explanation: Antigenic shift occurs when two different influenza strains co-infect the same host cell, leading to reassortment of their segmented RNA genomes. This creates novel hemagglutinin or neuraminidase surface antigens to which the human population has no immunity, causing pandemics.

question: A 68-year-old active woman being treated for a complicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa urinary tract infection presents to the clinic complaining of sudden onset left ankle pain and swelling. Examination reveals exquisite tenderness over the Achilles tendon, and Thompson test is weakly positive. Which antibiotic class prescribed for her infection is directly associated with tendonitis and tendon rupture? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-620]
explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV. They carry a black box warning for tendonitis and tendon rupture (most commonly the Achilles tendon), especially in elderly patients, organ transplant recipients, and those taking corticosteroids.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #621]: Which autoimmune connective tissue disorder presents with heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and symmetrical proximal muscle weakness with anti-Jo-1 antibodies?
explanation: Dermatomyositis is a CD4+ T cell-mediated perimysial autoimmune inflammatory myopathy. Clinical hallmarks include proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and shawl sign. Lab findings include elevated CK and positive anti-Jo-1 or anti-Mi-2 antibodies.

question: A 32-year-old non-smoking male accountant presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and wheezing. Family history reveals a maternal uncle who died of liver cirrhosis in his 40s. Chest CT demonstrates panacinar emphysema predominantly involving the lower lobes of both lungs. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules within hepatocytes. A deficiency of which circulating protein causes this combined pulmonary and hepatic pathology? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-622]
explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ genotype) results in uninhibited neutrophil elastase activity, destroying lung parenchyma (panacinar emphysema, lower lobe predominant). Misfolded AAT protein accumulates in liver endoplasmic reticulum, presenting as PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules and liver cirrhosis.

question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #987]: Which mechanism of genetic exchange in influenza viruses (segmented RNA genome) leads to major antigenic shifts responsible for global pandemics?

question: A 68-year-old active woman being treated for a complicated Pseudomonas aeruginosa urinary tract infection presents to the clinic complaining of sudden onset left ankle pain and swelling. question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #989]: Which autoimmune connective tissue disorder presents with heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, and symmetrical proximal muscle weakness with anti-Jo-1 antibodies?

question: A 32-year-old non-smoking male accountant presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and wheezing. Family history reveals a maternal uncle who died of liver cirrhosis in his 40s. Chest CT demonstrates panacinar emphysema predominantly involving the lower lobes of both lungs. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules within hepatocytes. A deficiency of which circulating protein causes this combined pulmonary and hepatic pathology? [Unique Exam Code USMLE-UB3-990]
explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ genotype) results in uninhibited neutrophil elastase activity, destroying lung parenchyma (panacinar emphysema, lower lobe predominant). question: [High-Yield Clinical Concept #991]: Which personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, alongside marked impulsivity and splitting defense mechanisms?

question: An 18-year-old woman is evaluated for lower abdominal distension and pelvic pain. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a 9 cm solid ovarian mass. Serum beta-hCG is mildly elevated, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is markedly increased, while AFP is normal. Histopathology of the resected tumor demonstrates sheets of large uniform cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm and central round nuclei separated by fibrous septa infiltrated with lymphocytes ('fried egg' appearance).
